gene_editing.abstract: Statistics > Methodology arXiv:2611.03255 (stat) [Submitted on 2 Nov 2026] Title: Conditional independence testing through marginal permutation Authors: Jiahao Ai , Ziang Niu View a PDF of the paper titled Conditional independence testing through marginal permutation, by Jiahao Ai and Ziang Niu View PDF HTML (experimental) Abstract: Marginal permutation is exact for testing marginal independence but generally invalid for conditional independence because it breaks the dependence between the exposure ($\bm X$) and covariates ($\bm Z$). In this paper, we show that empirical studentization can nevertheless make this deliberately misspecified resampling scheme asymptotically valid for important conditional independence tests based on scores. The resulting procedures are novel in the sense that they are valid in finite samples when the exposure is marginally independent of the outcome ($\bm Y$) and covariates, and asymptotically valid under the broader conditional independence null, $\bm X\indep \bm Y\mid \bm Z$, subject to method-specific conditions. For generalized linear model scores, separately studentizing the observed and permuted scores yields validity under a correctly specified null mean despite \emph{arbitrary} conditional variance misspecification. Moreover, the permutation calibration also applies to tests based on generalized and projected covariance measures. Their validity accommodates machine learning nuisance estimates under a condition on the stability of refitting after permutation, for which we provide sufficient conditions for common regression learners. Permutation calibration preserves first-order local power while better capturing the finite-sample discreteness and skewness induced by sparse observations. Simulations and single-cell CRISPR screen analysis show substantial calibration gains with our methods when effective sample size is small. Quantitative Biology > Genomics arXiv:2611.03806 (q-bio) [Submitted on 2 Nov 2026] Title: BEND 2.0: Benchmarking the Capabilities Needed to Design DNA Authors: Andreas Bjerregaard , Rachael DeVries , Dionysia Danai Brilli , Panagiotis Antoniadis , Yan Li , Anders Krogh , Wouter Boomsma , Ole Winther , Frederikke Isa Marin View a PDF of the paper titled BEND 2.0: Benchmarking the Capabilities Needed to Design DNA, by Andreas Bjerregaard and 8 other authors View PDF HTML (experimental) Abstract: Genomic foundation models are increasingly used to propose DNA sequences and edits. But successful design requires capabilities that current benchmarks do not measure. Here we introduce BEND 2.0 (BENchmark for DNA language models), which tests how well models predict the effects of DNA changes and whether these predictions can guide sequence design. Across eight tasks built on five experimental datasets, we find that model choice and how representations are accessed both affect performance. Linear readouts fitted to frozen representations can match or exceed models' native outputs, and functional post-training substantially improves the models' capabilities. Linear readouts transfer well across experimental assays and genes, suggesting that models capture functional patterns beyond the data used to fit individual predictors. At the same time, strong prediction of average effects can conceal weaker prediction of context-specific effects, and accurate prediction of combined mutation effects does not imply accurate prediction of their interactions. In design tasks, model predictions can reduce the number of candidates needed to find a desired response, but still leave substantial room for better design choices, particularly for context-specific and multi-cell objectives. Our benchmark reveals that genomic models now display signs of general utility but have yet to saturate on performance in even simple tasks. Abstract RNA predates cells, but today it “lives” inside them. Most current RNA is short-lived, folded, and often edited from its chromosomal origins, but it governs its own phenotypes. Our guiding question for this article was: How did RNA adjust its life when the RNA world era came to an end? RNA has its practical execution side in the whole-cell systems setup, serving critical functions in metabolism, compartmentalization, and in the RNA–DNA–PROTEIN network, coupling information handling and different events of macromolecule production into a self-sustaining loop. Aligning with current views of cooperation, we find that RNA life is distributed across a population of information-bearing entities persisting by compatibility, with DNA serving as a long-term memory and proteins offering the catalytic reach. We suggest that the reproduction–survival (R/S) axis, relevant to higher organisms, is also manifested by RNA in many forms, including RNA primers, mRNAs, tRNAs, and rRNAs. Each of these has contrasting, highly adapted molecular phenotypes. Ultimately, we wish to emphasize the evolutionary narrative where “RNA did not lose” in exchange for DNA genes or otherwise. Ultimately, RNA just changed strategy, and in its various forms, it has an active and critically important presence in all cells at all times.
